Rules:
- Input is a UTF-8 string.
- Records are separated by `\n` or `\r\n`. A bare `\r` not followed by `\n` is an error.
- Fields in a record are separated by commas.
- A field may be quoted with double quotes. A quoted field starts and ends with `"`.
- Inside a quoted field, commas, newlines, and carriage returns are literal characters.
- Two consecutive double quotes inside a quoted field represent one literal double quote.
- Outside a quoted field, a double quote is only allowed as the first character of a field. A double quote elsewhere in an unquoted field is an error.
- After the closing quote of a quoted field, the next character must be a comma, a newline, or the end of input. Any other character is an error.
- If the input ends while a quoted field is still open, return an error.
- Empty input returns an empty vector.
- A trailing newline does not create an extra empty record.
- An empty line is a record containing one empty field.
- Empty fields are allowed. For example, `a,,b` has three fields.
- Whitespace is preserved exactly; fields are not trimmed.
- Different records may have different numbers of fields.

Errors:
- `CsvError::UnclosedQuotedField`
- `CsvError::UnexpectedQuote`
- `CsvError::UnexpectedCharacterAfterQuote`
- `CsvError::InvalidLineEnding`

# Instructions

In this exercise you will implement a small memoized Fibonacci calculator.

Create a public type named `MemoizedFibonacci` with these methods:

- `new() -> Self`: creates an empty cache. It starts with zero computed values.
- `fib(&mut self, n: usize) -> u64`: returns the `n`th Fibonacci number, where `fib(0) == 0` and `fib(1) == 1`. The first time a value is requested, compute and cache it. Every later request for an already cached `n` must return the cached value without recomputing it.
- `computed_count(&self) -> usize`: returns how many distinct Fibonacci values have been computed so far, counting cache misses only. A cache hit does not change this count.
- `cached_value(&self, n: usize) -> Option<u64>`: returns `Some(value)` only if `n` has already been computed and stored, otherwise `None`.

Because computing `fib(n)` recursively also requires all smaller Fibonacci values, after a successful call to `fib(n)` the values from `0` through `n` are cached. Requesting a value never removes or changes existing cached values. You may assume `n` is at most 50, so the result fits in `u64`.

# Instructions

Implement a parser for a small shell-like command line.

Expose these public items:

- `Command` with public fields `program: String`, `args: Vec<String>`, and `options: Vec<(String, Option<String>)>`.
- `ParseError` with variants `EmptyInput`, `EmptyProgram`, `UnterminatedQuote`, `InvalidEscape(char)`, `InvalidOption`, and `InvalidOptionName`.
- `pub fn parse_command(input: &str) -> Result<Command, ParseError>`.

Parsing rules:

- Any Unicode whitespace outside quotes separates tokens and is ignored.
- Outside quotes, `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the input. It also ends the current token. For example, `cmd foo#bar` produces program `cmd` and argument `foo`.
- A token is made from adjacent bare fragments and double-quoted strings. Adjacent fragments are concatenated without separators. Bare characters are any characters other than whitespace, `#`, or `"`.
- A double-quoted string starts and ends with `"`. Inside it, the only valid escapes are `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, and `\t`. Any other backslash escape returns `InvalidEscape(c)` where `c` is the character after the backslash. Inside a quoted string, a backslash immediately before the end of input, or any missing closing quote, returns `UnterminatedQuote`.
- An empty quoted string `""` is allowed. It can be the whole token, producing an empty token, or contribute nothing to a larger token.
- The first token is the program. If there are no tokens, return `EmptyInput`. If the first token is empty, return `EmptyProgram`.
- Each remaining token that starts with `--` is an option. All other remaining tokens are positional arguments, collected in `args` in the order they appear.
- For an option, remove the leading `--`. If nothing remains, return `InvalidOption`. Split the remainder at the first `=` if present. The part before `=` is the option name; the part after it is the value, which may be empty. If there is no `=`, the value is `None`. If the name is empty, return `InvalidOption`. The name must contain only ASCII letters, ASCII digits, `_`, or `-`; otherwise return `InvalidOptionName`.
- Options are collected in `options` in the order they appear. A flag has value `None`; an assignment such as `--out=` has value `Some("")`. Empty positional arguments are allowed when created by `""`.
- Options and positional arguments are stored in separate vectors; their relative order is not preserved.

# Instructions

Implement a calendar module for the proleptic Gregorian calendar. "Proleptic" means the leap-year rules are applied to every year, including year zero and negative years.

A year is a leap year when it is divisible by 4, unless it is divisible by 100 but not by 400.

## `Weekday`

An enum with the seven variants `Monday`, `Tuesday`, `Wednesday`, `Thursday`, `Friday`, `Saturday` and `Sunday`, in that order.

## `Date`

Holds a year (`i32`), a month (`u32`, 1-12) and a day (`u32`). Two dates are equal when their year, month and day are equal; ordering is chronological. The fields are private, so a valid `Date` can only come from `Date::new` or one of the other constructors.

### `Date::new(year, month, day) -> Option<Date>`

Returns `Some` for a real calendar date and `None` when the month is not in 1..=12 or the day is not in 1..=the number of days in that month. For example 29 February of a common year, 31 April and day zero are all rejected.

### Accessors

`year() -> i32`, `month() -> u32` and `day() -> u32` return the stored parts.

### `days_in_month() -> u32`

The number of days in the date's month, taking leap years into account.

### `weekday() -> Weekday`

The day of the week. In this calendar 1 January of year 1 is a Monday.

### `add_days(days: i64) -> Date`

Returns the date that is `days` days later; a negative argument moves backwards. The result is always a valid date, so adding one day to the last day of a month rolls over into the next month, and adding one day to 31 December rolls over into the next year.

### `days_until(other: Date) -> i64`

The number of days from `self` to `other`, positive when `other` is later and negative when it is earlier. A date has zero days until itself.

### `iso_week() -> (i32, u32)`

The ISO 8601 week date as a pair of ISO year and week number. Weeks run Monday to Sunday, week 1 is the week containing the first Thursday of the calendar year, and there is no week 0. Near New Year the ISO year can be the year before or after the calendar year: 1 January 2021 belongs to ISO week 53 of 2020, and 31 December 2019 belongs to ISO week 1 of 2020.

### `Date::from_iso_week(year, week, weekday) -> Option<Date>`

The inverse operation: the date in ISO year `year`, ISO week `week`, on `weekday`. Returns `None` when `week` is 0 or larger than the number of ISO weeks that year actually has. The returned date may lie in a different calendar year than `year`.

### `Date::nth_weekday(year, month, weekday, n) -> Option<Date>`

The `n`th occurrence of `weekday` inside the given month. Positive `n` counts from the start of the month (1 is the first such weekday, 2 the second, and so on); negative `n` counts from the end (-1 is the last such weekday, -2 the one before it). Returns `None` when the month is invalid, when `n` is 0, or when the requested occurrence does not exist; a month contains at most five of any weekday.

## `weeks_in_iso_year(year) -> u32`

The number of ISO weeks in the given ISO year, either 52 or 53. A year has 53 ISO weeks when 1 January is a Thursday, or when the year is a leap year and 1 January is a Wednesday.

# Instructions

Implement the ADFGVX fractionating transposition cipher.

Define a public error type:

`pub enum CipherError { EmptyColumnKey, InvalidCiphertext }`

`CipherError` must derive `Debug`, `PartialEq`, and `Eq`.

Provide exactly these public functions:

`pub fn encode(plaintext: &str, square_key: &str, column_key: &str) -> Result<String, CipherError>`

`pub fn decode(ciphertext: &str, square_key: &str, column_key: &str) -> Result<String, CipherError>`

## Normalization

For plaintext and square_key, uppercase ASCII letters and keep only `A`-`Z` and `0`-`9`; discard everything else. For column_key, uppercase ASCII letters and keep only `A`-`Z`; discard everything else. If the normalized column_key is empty, return `Err(CipherError::EmptyColumnKey)` for both functions. This error takes precedence over empty text. An empty normalized plaintext or ciphertext encodes or decodes to the empty string. The cipher never preserves spaces, punctuation, or original case.

## Square

The 36 symbols are `ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789`. Build a 6 by 6 square by taking unique characters from the normalized square_key in order, then appending any missing symbols in the order just given. Each symbol's position is its row-major index: row `index / 6`, column `index % 6`.

## Encoding

For each normalized plaintext character, look up its row and column in the square. Convert each row and column number 0 through 5 to `A`, `D`, `F`, `G`, `V`, `X` respectively, and append the row symbol followed by the column symbol. This fractionated text contains only ADFGVX letters.

Apply a columnar transposition using the normalized column_key. Let `k` be the length of the column key. Write the fractionated text into rows of `k` columns from left to right and top to bottom. The last row may be short. Sort the original column indices by their key letters, using the original index to break ties, and read the columns in that order from top to bottom. Return the concatenation.

## Decoding

Normalize ciphertext by uppercasing ASCII and keeping only `A`, `D`, `F`, `G`, `V`, `X`; discard all other characters. If the resulting length is odd, return `Err(CipherError::InvalidCiphertext)`. Reverse the columnar transposition: compute the number of rows and the height of each original column from the transposed length and key length, split the ciphertext into column segments in sorted-key order, then read the grid row by row. Finally, read the fractionated text in pairs of ADFGVX symbols, map each pair back to a square position, and append the square symbol.

The empty ciphertext with a valid column key decodes to the empty string. Decoding never restores discarded punctuation, spaces, or original case; it returns only uppercase `A`-`Z` and `0`-`9`.

# Instructions

A ring buffer is a fixed-capacity FIFO queue backed by circular storage.

Implement a generic `RingBuffer<T>` with the following behavior:

- `RingBuffer::new(capacity)` creates an empty buffer with the given capacity. Capacity must be greater than zero; `new(0)` must panic with a message containing the word `capacity`.
- `capacity()` returns the buffer capacity.
- `len()` returns the number of stored values.
- `is_empty()` returns whether the buffer contains no values.
- `is_full()` returns whether the buffer contains exactly `capacity` values.
- `write(value)` appends a value to the back. If the buffer is full, return `Err(value)` and leave the buffer unchanged. Otherwise store the value and return `Ok(())`.
- `overwrite(value)` appends a value to the back even when full. If full, discard the oldest value first. If empty or not full, behave like a successful `write`. This method never returns an error.
- `read()` removes and returns the oldest value, or `None` if the buffer is empty.
- `peek()` returns a reference to the oldest value without removing it, or `None` if the buffer is empty.
- `clear()` removes all values but keeps the same capacity.

Values are ordered oldest to newest. The buffer must work for any `T`, including types that are not `Clone`. Indices must wrap modulo the capacity, so repeated fill, read, and overwrite cycles work correctly, including capacity one.

# Instructions

Implement the Bifid cipher. Your crate must expose two functions:

encode(keyword: &str, period: usize, message: &str) -> String

decode(keyword: &str, period: usize, message: &str) -> String

The cipher uses a 5 by 5 Polybius square. Build the square from the keyword as follows:

- Consider only ASCII alphabetic characters in the keyword.
- Convert letters to uppercase.
- Treat J as I; the square never contains J.
- Keep the first occurrence of each letter.
- Append the remaining uppercase letters A through Z, omitting J, in alphabetical order.
- If the keyword has no usable letters, the square is the standard A-Z square with J omitted.

Message normalization:

- Consider only ASCII alphabetic characters; ignore spaces, digits, punctuation, and any non-ASCII characters.
- Convert to uppercase.
- Treat J as I.
- The output is a single continuous uppercase string with no separators. If the normalized message is empty, return an empty string.

The period is the number of normalized letters in each block. A period of 0 means use one block for the whole normalized message. A positive period splits the letters into consecutive blocks of that size; the final block may be shorter. A period larger than the number of normalized letters therefore produces one block.

Encoding one block:

- Map each plaintext letter to a row and column in the square, using zero-based indices 0 through 4 from the top-left.
- Write all row indices in order, followed by all column indices in order.
- Group the resulting digit sequence into consecutive pairs. Each pair is a row and column coordinate; replace each pair with the square letter at that coordinate.

Decoding one block:

- Map each ciphertext letter to its row and column, producing two digits per letter in row-then-column order.
- A block of n ciphertext letters produces 2n digits. Split this digit sequence into the first n digits and the last n digits.
- Pair the first row digit with the first column digit, the second row digit with the second column digit, and so on.
- Replace each pair with the square letter at that coordinate.

For both functions, split the normalized input into blocks before encoding or decoding, and concatenate the block results in order.

After choosing winners, omit every key whose winning record is a tombstone. Return exactly one record per surviving key, ordered by key ascending. Empty inputs, empty logs, duplicate identical records, and keys that appear in many logs must all be handled. A lower-revision live record must not resurrect a key when a higher-revision tombstone exists.

Implement an inventory tracker for a small network of warehouses. Each item is identified by a SKU and has a name, a unit price in cents, and a reorder level. Each warehouse tracks on-hand and reserved quantities for an item. Available stock is on hand minus reserved.

The public API is:

- `Inventory::new()` creates an empty inventory.
- `register_item(sku, name, unit_price_cents)` registers a new item. Reject an empty SKU with `InvalidSku`, an empty name with `InvalidName`, and an already registered SKU with `DuplicateSku(sku)`. A price of zero is allowed.
- `set_reorder_level(sku, level)` changes the item's reorder level.
- `receive(sku, warehouse, quantity)` adds stock to a warehouse. The warehouse is created if needed.
- `reserve(sku, warehouse, quantity)` reserves available stock without changing on-hand stock. Fail with `InsufficientStock { available, requested }` when there is not enough available stock.
- `release(sku, warehouse, quantity)` releases reserved stock. Fail with `InsufficientReserved { reserved, requested }` when there is not enough reserved stock.
- `ship(sku, warehouse, quantity)` fulfills reserved stock by reducing both on-hand and reserved quantities by the same amount. Fail with `InsufficientReserved { reserved, requested }` when there is not enough reserved stock.
- `adjust(sku, warehouse, delta)` changes on-hand stock by a signed amount. A positive delta adds stock. A negative delta may only consume available stock; if its magnitude exceeds available stock, fail with `InsufficientStock { available, requested }` where requested is the magnitude. Reserved stock is unchanged.
- `transfer(sku, from, to, quantity)` moves available stock from one warehouse to another. The destination warehouse is created if needed. Reserved stock at the source is unchanged. Fail with `SameWarehouse` when `from == to`, and with `InsufficientStock { available, requested }` when the source lacks enough available stock.
- `available(sku, warehouse)` returns on-hand minus reserved for that warehouse, or 0 for a warehouse with no recorded stock.
- `total_on_hand(sku)` sums on-hand quantities across all warehouses, including reserved units.
- `low_stock()` returns a sorted `Vec<String>` of SKUs whose total available stock across all warehouses is less than or equal to the item's reorder level. The default reorder level is 0.
- `total_value_cents()` sums `on_hand * unit_price_cents` across all items and warehouses.

For operations that take a quantity, zero is rejected with `InvalidQuantity`. For `adjust`, a delta of zero is rejected with `InvalidQuantity`. An unknown SKU returns `UnknownSku(sku)`. A warehouse with no recorded stock has zero on hand and zero reserved.

`InventoryError` has these variants:

- `DuplicateSku(String)`
- `UnknownSku(String)`
- `InvalidSku`
- `InvalidName`
- `InvalidQuantity`
- `InsufficientStock { available: u32, requested: u32 }`
- `InsufficientReserved { reserved: u32, requested: u32 }`
- `SameWarehouse`

# Instructions

Implement a small library for integer set operations. Each input is a slice of signed integers that may be unsorted and may contain duplicates. Treat each slice as a mathematical set: duplicates are ignored and input order does not matter. Every returned vector must contain each value at most once and must be sorted in ascending order.

Implement the following public functions:

- `pub fn union(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>` returns the values that appear in `a` or `b`.
- `pub fn intersection(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>` returns the values that appear in both `a` and `b`.
- `pub fn difference(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>` returns the values that appear in `a` but not in `b`.
- `pub fn symmetric_difference(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>` returns the values that appear in exactly one of `a` or `b`.
- `pub fn is_subset(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> bool` returns true when every distinct value of `a` appears in `b`.
- `pub fn is_disjoint(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> bool` returns true when `a` and `b` share no distinct value.

Edge cases:

- Empty slices are valid sets. `is_subset(&[], &[])` and `is_subset(&[], &[1])` are true. `is_disjoint(&[], &[1])` is true.
- Duplicates count only once. For example, the intersection of `[1, 1, 2]` and `[2, 2, 3]` is `[2]`.
- Negative values are allowed.
- Difference is directional: `difference(a, b)` can differ from `difference(b, a)`.
- For `is_subset`, the first argument is the candidate subset of the second argument.
- All returned vectors must be sorted ascending and contain no duplicates.

# Instructions

Implement `merge_circular_intervals`, which merges inclusive intervals on a circular integer domain.

The domain contains the values `0` through `domain_size - 1`. If `domain_size` is zero, return an empty list.

Each interval is a `(start, end)` pair. If `start <= end`, the interval contains the values from `start` through `end` in increasing order. If `start > end`, it wraps around: it contains `start` through `domain_size - 1` followed by `0` through `end`. Both endpoints are included.

Intervals that overlap, touch, or are adjacent on the circle must be merged into the largest possible clockwise run. Two inclusive intervals are adjacent when there is no missing value between them; for example, `(1, 3)` and `(4, 6)` merge, and `(8, 9)` and `(0, 2)` merge on a domain of size 10.

Return the merged intervals in ascending order by start. Each returned interval must be non-overlapping and non-adjacent to the others. A merged interval that wraps must be represented as `(start, end)` with `start > end`. If the merged intervals cover every value in the domain, return exactly `(0, domain_size - 1)`.

Ignore any input interval whose start or end is not less than `domain_size`. If no valid intervals remain, return an empty list.

# Instructions

Implement a small bank account simulation in Rust. Money is represented as integer cents using i64. The public API must be available from the same file as the tests.

Public types:
- AccountStatus has variants Open, Frozen, Closed.
- EntryKind has variants Deposit, Withdrawal, TransferIn { from: u32 }, TransferOut { to: u32 }, and Interest.
- Entry has public fields kind: EntryKind, amount: i64, and balance_after: i64. The amount is signed: positive for credits, negative for debits.
- AccountInfo has public fields id: u32, owner: String, balance: i64, overdraft_limit: i64, and status: AccountStatus.
- BankError has variants AccountNotFound, AccountAlreadyExists, AccountClosed, AccountFrozen, InvalidOwner, InvalidAmount, InvalidRate, InvalidOverdraftLimit, OverdraftLimitTooLow, InsufficientFunds, SameAccount, InvalidState, and NonZeroBalance.

Required Bank methods:
- new() -> Bank
- open_account(&mut self, id: u32, owner: &str) -> Result<(), BankError>
- close_account(&mut self, id: u32) -> Result<(), BankError>
- freeze_account(&mut self, id: u32) -> Result<(), BankError>
- unfreeze_account(&mut self, id: u32) -> Result<(), BankError>
- set_overdraft_limit(&mut self, id: u32, limit: i64) -> Result<(), BankError>
- deposit(&mut self, id: u32, amount: i64) -> Result<i64, BankError>
- withdraw(&mut self, id: u32, amount: i64) -> Result<i64, BankError>
- transfer(&mut self, from: u32, to: u32, amount: i64) -> Result<(), BankError>
- balance(&self, id: u32) -> Result<i64, BankError>
- account_info(&self, id: u32) -> Result<AccountInfo, BankError>
- history(&self, id: u32) -> Result<Vec<Entry>, BankError>
- apply_interest(&mut self, rate_bps: i64) -> Result<(), BankError>

Behavior:
- Opening an account requires a unique id and an owner containing at least one non-whitespace character. The owner is stored exactly as provided. Duplicate ids return AccountAlreadyExists before owner validation. Empty or whitespace-only owners return InvalidOwner.
- New accounts start Open with balance 0 and overdraft limit 0.
- freeze_account changes Open to Frozen. Freezing a Frozen account returns AccountFrozen. Freezing a Closed account returns AccountClosed.
- unfreeze_account changes Frozen to Open. Unfreezing an Open account returns InvalidState. Unfreezing a Closed account returns AccountClosed.
- close_account succeeds only for an Open account with balance 0, changing it to Closed. Frozen returns AccountFrozen, Closed returns AccountClosed, and nonzero balance returns NonZeroBalance.
- set_overdraft_limit requires an Open account. Closed returns AccountClosed and Frozen returns AccountFrozen. A negative limit returns InvalidOverdraftLimit. A limit smaller than the absolute value of a negative balance returns OverdraftLimitTooLow.
- For deposit, withdraw, and transfer, amount must be greater than 0 or InvalidAmount is returned. For deposit and withdraw, amount validation happens before account lookup. For transfer, amount validation happens first, then from == to returns SameAccount.
- Deposits and withdrawals require an Open account. Frozen returns AccountFrozen and Closed returns AccountClosed.
- Withdrawals may make the balance negative, but not below negative overdraft_limit. Otherwise return InsufficientFunds.
- Transfers check the source account, then the destination account, then source funds. Both accounts must exist and be Open. Frozen returns AccountFrozen and Closed returns AccountClosed. If any check fails, no balances or histories change. A successful transfer debits the source and credits the destination.
- Frozen accounts block deposits, withdrawals, transfers in or out, closing, and interest. Queries and freeze/unfreeze still work.
- balance, account_info, and history work for Open, Frozen, and Closed accounts. Missing ids return AccountNotFound.
- Each successful deposit appends an Entry with kind Deposit and a positive amount.
- Each successful withdrawal appends an Entry with kind Withdrawal and a negative amount.
- A successful transfer appends TransferOut { to } with a negative amount to the source account and TransferIn { from } with a positive amount to the destination account.
- apply_interest requires rate_bps >= 0 or InvalidRate is returned. For every Open account with positive balance, interest equals floor(balance * rate_bps / 10000). If interest is greater than 0, credit it and append an Entry with kind Interest. Frozen and Closed accounts are skipped. If interest rounds to 0, no entry is appended. Negative rates change nothing.
- Histories are ordered oldest first. Failed operations do not append entries. Opening accounts, changing status, and changing overdraft limits do not append entries. Closed accounts retain their histories.

# Instructions

Implement a first-in-first-out queue of signed 64-bit integers (`i64`) that also reports the minimum and maximum values currently in the queue. All operations must run in amortized O(1) time; scanning all queued values for `minimum` or `maximum` will not satisfy the requirement.

Create `pub struct MinMaxQueue` with the following methods:

- `pub fn new() -> Self`
- `pub fn enqueue(&mut self, value: i64)`
- `pub fn dequeue(&mut self) -> Option<i64>`
- `pub fn peek(&self) -> Option<i64>`
- `pub fn minimum(&self) -> Option<i64>`
- `pub fn maximum(&self) -> Option<i64>`
- `pub fn len(&self) -> usize`
- `pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool`

Behavior:

- A new queue is empty.
- `enqueue` appends a value to the back of the queue.
- `dequeue` removes and returns the value at the front, or `None` if the queue is empty.
- `peek` returns the front value without removing it, or `None` if the queue is empty.
- `minimum` returns the smallest queued value, or `None` if the queue is empty.
- `maximum` returns the largest queued value, or `None` if the queue is empty.
- `len` returns the number of queued values.
- `is_empty` returns `true` exactly when the queue contains no values.
- Duplicate values must be preserved and counted normally.
- Values may be negative, zero, or any valid `i64`, including `i64::MIN` and `i64::MAX`.
- FIFO ordering must be exact across any mixture of operations.

Use only the Rust standard library. Two stacks can represent the queue, and each stack entry can cache the minimum and maximum needed for that stack's contents.

# Instructions

Implement two parallel bit operations on unsigned 64-bit integers. Bits are numbered from 0 at the least significant bit.

The function extract_bits(value, mask) must collect the bits of value whose positions are selected by mask. The selected bits are packed into the low-order bits of the result, preserving their original least-significant-to-most-significant order. Bits of value that are not selected by mask are ignored. For example, extract_bits(0b1101, 0b1010) returns 0b10 because mask selects bits 1 and 3, whose values are 0 and 1.

The function deposit_bits(value, mask) performs the inverse operation. It takes the low-order bits of value in least-significant-to-most-significant order and places them into the positions selected by mask, also in least-significant-to-most-significant order. All other result bits must be 0. If value contains more bits than mask has set bits, the extra high bits are ignored. For example, deposit_bits(0b10, 0b1010) returns 0b1000 because the low bit 0 goes to mask bit 1 and the next bit 1 goes to mask bit 3.

Edge cases: a mask of 0 must return 0 for both functions. A mask of u64::MAX must make extract_bits return value unchanged, while deposit_bits must also return value unchanged. All u64 inputs are valid and neither function should panic.

# Instructions

Implement an AVL tree set named `AvlTree<T>` for any `T: Ord + Clone`. The tree stores unique values in ascending order and must remain height-balanced after every successful insertion or removal.

Provide these methods:

- `AvlTree::new() -> Self`
- `insert(&mut self, value: T)`: inserts `value`. If it is already present, the tree must remain unchanged.
- `remove(&mut self, value: &T) -> bool`: removes `value` and returns `true` if it was present. If it is absent, return `false` and leave the tree unchanged.
- `contains(&self, value: &T) -> bool`
- `len(&self) -> usize`: number of unique stored values.
- `is_empty(&self) -> bool`
- `height(&self) -> usize`: empty tree has height `0`; a single node has height `1`.
- `in_order(&self) -> Vec<T>`: returns clones of all values in ascending order.

Requirements:

- After every insert or successful remove, every node must satisfy the AVL balance condition: the absolute difference between the heights of its left and right subtrees is at most `1`.
- Duplicate insertion must not change `len`, `height`, or traversal.
- Removing a missing value must not change the tree.
- Removing a node with two children must use the minimum value from its right subtree as the replacement.
- No exact tree shape is required; any valid AVL tree representation is acceptable.
- Use only the Rust standard library.

# Instructions

Implement `tokenize` for a small expression language.

`pub fn tokenize(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<Token>, TokenizeError>`

Tokens are returned in input order. Skip any Unicode whitespace between tokens.

Numbers
- `Token::Number(i64)` is a sequence of one or more ASCII digits.
- No sign, decimal point, or underscores are part of a number.
- Leading zeros are allowed and parsed normally.
- If the literal does not fit in `i64`, return `InvalidNumber(literal, start_byte_index)`.

Identifiers
- `Token::Ident(String)` starts with an ASCII letter or `_`.
- It continues with ASCII letters, digits, or `_`.

Strings
- `Token::Str(String)` starts and ends with `"`.
- Supported escapes: `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\0`.
- Any other backslash escape returns `InvalidEscape(char, byte_index_of_escape_char)`.
- If the closing quote is missing, return `UnterminatedString(byte_index_of_opening_quote)`.

Operators
- `+` `Op::Plus`
- `-` `Op::Minus`
- `*` `Op::Star`
- `/` `Op::Slash`
- `%` `Op::Percent`
- `=` `Op::Assign`
- `==` `Op::Eq`
- `!=` `Op::Ne`
- `<` `Op::Lt`
- `<=` `Op::Le`
- `>` `Op::Gt`
- `>=` `Op::Ge`
- `!` `Op::Not`
- `&&` `Op::And`
- `||` `Op::Or`
- `->` `Op::Arrow`
Use longest match first. A lone `&` or `|` is an unexpected character.

Punctuation
- `(` `Token::LParen`
- `)` `Token::RParen`
- `{` `Token::LBrace`
- `}` `Token::RBrace`
- `,` `Token::Comma`
- `;` `Token::Semicolon`
- `:` `Token::Colon`

Comments
- `//` skips to the end of the line or end of input.
- `/*` skips to the next `*/`. Block comments are not nested.
- If EOF occurs before `*/`, return `UnterminatedComment(byte_index_of_opening_slash)`.

Errors
- `UnexpectedCharacter(char, byte_index)` for any other character.
- Byte indices are zero-based positions in the original input.

# Instructions

Implement a running-totals ledger that supports adding deltas, undo/redo, and checkpoints.

The ledger starts empty with current total 0. A delta is an i64 added to the current total. Only deltas in the active history affect queries. Undone deltas are held on a redo stack; rolled-back deltas are discarded.

Required API:
- RunningTotals::new() creates an empty ledger.
- push(delta) appends delta to active history, clears redo, and returns the new current total.
- extend(deltas) accepts any IntoIterator<Item = i64> and pushes each item in order. A non-empty extension clears redo through those pushes. An empty extension changes nothing, including redo.
- current() returns the sum of active deltas, or 0 when empty.
- len() returns the number of active deltas; is_empty() reports len == 0.
- total_after(events) returns Some(sum of the first events active deltas) when events <= len. total_after(0) is Some(0). If events > len return None.
- max_total() and min_total() return the maximum/minimum of 0 and all cumulative totals after each active event. An empty ledger returns 0 for both.
- checkpoint() returns the current len.
- rollback(checkpoint) succeeds when checkpoint <= len, truncates active history to that many deltas, clears redo, and returns Ok(()). If checkpoint > len return Err and leave the ledger unchanged.
- undo() removes the last active delta, places it on redo, and returns Some(new current total); if there is no active delta return None.
- redo() takes the most recently undone delta, appends it to active history, and returns Some(new current total); if redo is empty return None.
- clear() removes all active and redo history.

Edge cases: undo and redo do not clear each other; pushing or a successful rollback clears redo; rollback never creates redo entries. Queries ignore undone and rolled-back deltas. Assume all sums fit in i64.

The input may begin with one optional + or - sign. After an optional sign, it must contain at least one digit. An empty string, a lone +, or a lone - returns ConversionError::EmptyInput. Any character after the optional sign that is not a valid digit for from_base returns ConversionError::InvalidDigit containing that character exactly as it appeared. The input may be arbitrarily large, so do not rely on fixed-width integer types overflowing. The output uses uppercase letters for values above 9, has no plus sign, and has no leading zeros. # Instructions

Implement a course prerequisite graph as an adjacency map. Course names are strings. An edge points from a prerequisite to the course that depends on it; internally, each course records its direct prerequisites.

Public API:
- CourseGraph::new()
- add_course(&mut self, course: &str)
- add_prerequisite(&mut self, course: &str, prerequisite: &str)
- courses(&self) -> Vec<String>
- prerequisites_of(&self, course: &str) -> Vec<String>
- dependents_of(&self, course: &str) -> Vec<String>
- all_prerequisites(&self, course: &str) -> Vec<String>
- schedule(&self) -> Result<Vec<String>, Vec<String>>

Behavior:
- add_course ensures the course exists with no prerequisites. Adding an existing course does nothing.
- add_prerequisite ensures both courses exist and records that prerequisite must come before course. Duplicate additions do nothing. Self-prerequisites are allowed and create a cycle.
- courses returns all course names in ascending lexicographic order.
- prerequisites_of returns the direct prerequisites of course sorted ascending. An unknown course returns an empty vector.
- dependents_of returns the direct courses that list course as a prerequisite, sorted ascending. An unknown course returns an empty vector.
- all_prerequisites returns the sorted distinct courses reachable by following prerequisite edges from course, excluding the starting course itself even if a cycle reaches it. An unknown course returns an empty vector.
- schedule returns a valid order of all courses where every course appears after all of its direct prerequisites. Among all valid orders, return the lexicographically smallest one.
- If no valid order exists, schedule returns Err with the sorted names of all courses that remain after repeatedly removing courses with no remaining prerequisites. This includes courses in cycles and courses blocked by cycles.
- The empty graph schedules to Ok(empty vector).

All returned vectors are sorted ascending using Rust string ordering.

# Instructions

Implement a generic singly linked list type called `List<T>` that can hold any element type `T`. Provide the following public API:

- `List::new()` — creates a new, empty list.
- `push_front(&mut self, value: T)` — adds `value` to the front (head) of the list.
- `push_back(&mut self, value: T)` — adds `value` to the back (tail) of the list.
- `pop_front(&mut self) -> Option<T>` — removes the front element and returns it.
- `pop_back(&mut self) -> Option<T>` — removes the back element and returns it.
- `len(&self) -> usize` — returns the number of elements currently stored.
- `is_empty(&self) -> bool` — returns `true` if the list contains no elements.
- `reverse(&mut self)` — reverses the order of the elements in place.

## Behavior and edge cases

- A freshly created list is empty: `len()` returns `0` and `is_empty()` returns `true`.
- `pop_front` and `pop_back` on an empty list return `None` and leave the list unchanged.
- Removing the final remaining element with either `pop_front` or `pop_back` must leave the list empty (`is_empty()` is `true` and `len()` is `0`).
- Front and back operations may be freely interleaved. For example, after `push_back(1)`, `push_front(0)`, and `push_back(2)`, the order from front to back is `0, 1, 2`, so `pop_front` yields `0` and `pop_back` yields `2`.
- `reverse` on an empty list or a single-element list is a no-op: the list stays valid and its contents (or emptiness) are unchanged.
- Calling `reverse` twice restores the original order.
- `reverse` never changes `len()`.
- `len()` must remain accurate after every operation, and `is_empty()` must agree with `len() == 0`.
- Element types are opaque; the list must work for plain values such as integers and for owned types such as `String`.

Implement the list in safe Rust using only the standard library. Correctness of the described behavior matters more than asymptotic performance.

# Instructions

You are writing a small library of Gregorian calendar calculations for a scheduling service.

The calendar is the proleptic Gregorian calendar. Years start at 1 and are represented as `u32`. Months are 1-based (`1` is January, `12` is December) and days of the month are 1-based.

Implement the following public items in the crate root.

## Weekday

Provide a public enum named `Weekday` with exactly these variants, in this order: `Monday`, `Tuesday`, `Wednesday`, `Thursday`, `Friday`, `Saturday`, `Sunday`. It must derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq` and `Eq`.

## is_leap_year

`pub fn is_leap_year(year: u32) -> bool`

Returns true when the year is a leap year: divisible by 4, except for centuries, which are leap years only when divisible by 400. So 2024 and 2000 are leap years, while 1900 and 2023 are not.

## days_in_month

`pub fn days_in_month(year: u32, month: u32) -> u32`

The number of days in the given month of the given year. February has 29 days in a leap year and 28 otherwise. Panics if `month` is not in `1..=12`.

## day_of_week

`pub fn day_of_week(year: u32, month: u32, day: u32) -> Weekday`

The weekday of the given date, where 1 January of year 1 is a Monday. Panics if the year is 0 or the date does not exist in the calendar.

## nth_weekday

`pub fn nth_weekday(year: u32, month: u32, weekday: Weekday, n: i32) -> Option<u32>`

Returns the day of the month on which the `n`th occurrence of `weekday` falls.

- A positive `n` counts from the start of the month: `1` is the first such weekday, `2` the second, and so on.
- A negative `n` counts from the end of the month: `-1` is the last such weekday, `-2` the second to last, and so on.
- Return `None` when that occurrence does not exist in the month, for example the fifth Monday of a month that only has four, and also when `n` is 0.
- Panics if `month` is not in `1..=12`.

## easter_sunday

`pub fn easter_sunday(year: u32) -> (u32, u32)`

Returns the `(month, day)` of Easter Sunday in the Gregorian calendar, using the anonymous Gregorian computus. The result is always in March (month 3) or April (month 4). Easter Sunday 2024 is 31 March and Easter Sunday 2025 is 20 April.

## iso_week

`pub fn iso_week(year: u32, month: u32, day: u32) -> (u32, u32)`

Returns the `(iso_year, iso_week)` of the given date according to ISO 8601.

- Weeks start on Monday.
- Week 1 is the week that contains the first Thursday of the year.
- As a consequence, the opening days of January can belong to week 52 or 53 of the previous year, and the closing days of December can belong to week 1 of the next year, so the returned year is not always the year that was passed in.
- The returned week is always in `1..=53`.

Panics in the same situations as `day_of_week`.

# Instructions

Roman numerals are a numeral system that originated in ancient Rome and stayed in use throughout Europe well into the Middle Ages. They are written with letters of the Latin alphabet, each holding a fixed value:

- I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000

Modern usage writes a number with the largest symbols that fit, and uses six subtractive pairs so that a symbol never appears more than three times in a row: IV (4), IX (9), XL (40), XC (90), CD (400), CM (900).

Write two functions in `src/lib.rs`.

`pub fn to_roman(number: u32) -> String` returns the standard Roman numeral for a number. The input is always between 1 and 3999 inclusive, so no more than four thousand symbol values are ever needed.

`pub fn from_roman(roman: &str) -> Result<u32, String>` returns the value of a Roman numeral, or an error message if the input is not a valid standard Roman numeral.

Edge cases:

- An empty string is an error.
- Any character other than I, V, X, L, C, D, or M is an error, including lowercase letters and whitespace.
- Non-canonical arrangements are errors even when they can be read symbol by symbol: IIII, VV, VIIII, VX, IC, IM, XM, and the like.
- Values outside the range 1 to 3999 are errors, for example MMMM.
- Every valid numeral must round-trip: `from_roman(to_roman(n))` equals `Ok(n)` for each n from 1 to 3999.
- The text of an error message is never checked, only whether the result is `Ok` or `Err`.

Implement the function `compare_versions(left, right)`, which compares two dotted numeric version strings and returns `std::cmp::Ordering`.

Return `Less` when `left` is smaller than `right`, `Greater` when `left` is larger, and `Equal` when both versions represent the same value.

Version strings consist of one or more non-negative decimal segments separated by dots. Compare corresponding segments from left to right as numbers, not lexicographically.

Edge cases:
- Missing trailing segments are treated as zero, so `1.0` equals `1` and `1.0.0.0` equals `1`.

- An all-zero segment has value zero, so `0.0.0` equals `0`.
- Extra nonzero segments make a version larger, so `1.2.1` is greater than `1.2`.
- Segments may be arbitrarily long; compare them by numeric value without requiring fixed-size integer parsing.
- The first segment that differs determines the result. If all segments match after padding the shorter version with zeros, return `Equal`.

# Instructions

Implement three functions that group a slice of items by a key produced from each item.

The first function, `group_by`, takes a slice and a function that maps an item to its key, and returns a vector of `(key, items)` pairs. Groups appear in the order each key is first seen, and the items inside each group keep their original relative order. A key can appear in only one group.

The second function, `group_by_sorted`, does the same grouping but returns the pairs sorted in ascending order by key. Use the natural ordering of the key type (numeric for numbers, lexicographic for strings). Within-group order is still the original relative order.

The third function, `group_chunked`, accepts an extra `max_per_group` size. It groups exactly like `group_by` (first-appearance order for keys) and then splits each group into consecutive chunks of at most `max_per_group` items. All chunks belonging to one key are emitted together, in order, before moving on to the next key. A group whose length is less than or equal to the limit yields a single chunk. A limit of `0` means no splitting and yields one chunk per key.

All three functions are generic over the item type and key type. Item cloning is allowed. For `group_by` and `group_chunked` keys only need equality; for `group_by_sorted` keys need a total order and are returned in ascending order.

Edge cases: an empty input returns an empty vector for every function. Keys of the same value always land in the same group even if non-adjacent. Negative and zero numeric keys sort before positive ones in the sorted variant.

## Documents

A document is: optional whitespace, exactly one value, optional whitespace, end of input. Anything left over after that is an error.

Whitespace means space (U+0020), tab (U+0009), newline (U+000A) or carriage return (U+000D). No other character counts as whitespace.

## Values

A value is one of:

- `null`, producing `Json::Null`
- `true` or `false`, producing `Json::Bool`
- a number, producing `Json::Number`
- a string, producing `Json::String`
- an array, producing `Json::Array`
- an object, producing `Json::Object`

Keywords are written exactly in lower case.

## Numbers

- An optional leading `-`.
- An integer part that is either the single digit `0` or a digit `1`–`9` followed by any number of digits.
- An optional fraction: a `.` followed by at least one digit.
- An optional exponent: `e` or `E`, an optional `+` or `-`, then at least one digit.

So `01`, `-01`, `1.`, `.5`, `1e`, `+1` and a bare `-` are all errors. Convert the matched text with Rust's own `f64` parsing, so `1e3` becomes `1000.0`.

## Strings

A string is `"`, then any characters, then a closing `"`.

- The characters `"` and `\` and the control characters U+0000 through U+001F must be escaped; a raw control character inside a string is an error.
- These escapes are recognised: `\"`, `\\`, `\/`, `\b` (U+0008), `\f` (U+000C), `\n`, `\r`, `\t`.
- `\uXXXX` takes exactly four hexadecimal digits (either case) and inserts that code point.
- A high surrogate from `\uD800` to `\uDBFF` must be followed immediately by a low surrogate from `\uDC00` to `\uDFFF`; the pair decodes to one combined code point, so `"\uD83D\uDE00"` is the single character 😀.
- A lone or mismatched surrogate is an error.
- Non-ASCII characters may also appear literally in the string, as in `"héllo"`.
- An unterminated string, or a backslash at the end of the input, is an error.

## Arrays

An array is `[`, optional whitespace, then either `]` or one or more values separated by commas, then optional whitespace, then `]`. `[]` is valid. A trailing comma such as `[1,]` is an error.

## Objects

An object is `{`, optional whitespace, then either `}` or one or more `"key": value` pairs separated by commas, then optional whitespace, then `}`. Keys are always strings and accept the same escapes. `{}` is valid, and a trailing comma is an error. If the same key appears more than once, the last value wins (plain `BTreeMap::insert` behaviour).

## Errors

Return `Err` whenever the input does not match the grammar, including for empty input, whitespace-only input, a value followed by extra text, missing or misplaced separators, invalid escapes, and unterminated constructs.

`position` is a byte offset into `input`. It should be the index of the byte that could not be accepted, or `input.len()` when the input ended too early. For example, `"01"` reports position 1, `"[1,]"` reports position 3, `"{\"a\" 1}"` reports position 5, and the unterminated `"abc` reports position 4. The `message` field is free-form and is never inspected.

Implement the function `round_fraction(numerator: i64, denominator: i64, mode: RoundingMode) -> i64`.

The two integers describe the exact fraction `numerator / denominator`. Return the integer obtained by rounding that fraction according to `mode`. Do not use floating point arithmetic; the behavior must be exact for all integer inputs whose rounded result fits in `i64`.

`RoundingMode` has these variants:

- `Truncate`: round toward zero.
- `AwayFromZero`: round away from zero, so any nonzero fractional part increases the magnitude.
- `Ceiling`: round toward positive infinity.
- `Floor`: round toward negative infinity.
- `HalfUp`: round to the nearest integer; if the fraction is exactly halfway between two integers, round away from zero.
- `HalfDown`: round to the nearest integer; if the fraction is exactly halfway between two integers, round toward zero.
- `HalfEven`: round to the nearest integer; if the fraction is exactly halfway between two integers, round to the even integer.

If the fraction is already an integer, every mode returns that integer unchanged. A negative denominator is allowed and has the same value as moving the sign to the numerator. A denominator of zero must cause a panic.

# Instructions

Simulate a small bank. All money is handled as **integer cents** (`i64`); no floating point is involved anywhere. A balance may be negative when an account has an overdraft limit.

## Types

- `AccountId(pub u64)` — a public tuple struct identifying an account. New ids are issued as `1`, `2`, `3`, … in the order accounts are opened. An id is **never reused**, even after its account is closed.
- `BankError` — the error type returned by fallible operations, with these variants:
  - `AccountNotFound` — no open account has that id.
  - `InvalidAmount` — an amount was zero or negative, or an overdraft limit was negative.
  - `InsufficientFunds` — the operation would push the balance below the negative of the overdraft limit.
  - `SameAccount` — a transfer used the same account as source and destination.
  - `OutstandingDebt` — an account with a negative balance was asked to close.
- `Bank` — the bank itself.

## Operations

- `Bank::new()` — an empty bank with no accounts.
- `open_account(&mut self) -> AccountId` — creates an account with balance `0` and overdraft limit `0`, and returns its id.
- `account_count(&self) -> usize` — the number of currently open accounts.
- `balance(&self, id) -> Result<i64, BankError>` — the current balance in cents (may be negative).
- `deposit(&mut self, id, cents) -> Result<i64, BankError>` — adds money and returns the new balance. Rejects `cents <= 0` with `InvalidAmount`, then an unknown id with `AccountNotFound`.
- `withdraw(&mut self, id, cents) -> Result<i64, BankError>` — removes money and returns the new balance. Rejects `cents <= 0` with `InvalidAmount`, then an unknown id with `AccountNotFound`, then `InsufficientFunds` if `balance - cents < -overdraft_limit`. A failed withdrawal must leave the balance unchanged. Withdrawing exactly down to the overdraft limit succeeds.
- `set_overdraft_limit(&mut self, id, cents) -> Result<(), BankError>` — sets the overdraft limit. Rejects a negative limit with `InvalidAmount`, then an unknown id with `AccountNotFound`. A limit of `0` is legal and is the default.
- `transfer(&mut self, from, to, cents) -> Result<(), BankError>` — moves money between two accounts. Checks run in this order: `cents <= 0` → `InvalidAmount`; `from == to` → `SameAccount`; either account missing (`from` checked first) → `AccountNotFound`; source funds (same rule as withdrawal) → `InsufficientFunds`. A transfer is **atomic**: any error leaves both balances untouched, and on success the source is debited and the destination credited by the same amount.
- `apply_interest(&mut self, basis_points: u32) -> i64` — credits interest to every account whose balance is strictly positive. The interest is `balance * basis_points / 10_000`, computed with integer division (fractions of a cent are discarded). Accounts with a zero or negative balance, and accounts whose interest would round down to `0`, are left untouched. Returns the total interest credited across all accounts.
- `close_account(&mut self, id) -> Result<i64, BankError>` — closes an account and returns the balance that is paid out. Rejects an unknown id with `AccountNotFound` and an account whose balance is negative with `OutstandingDebt` (the account then stays open). Closing an account with a zero or positive balance succeeds and removes it, after which every operation on that id reports `AccountNotFound`. Closing does not affect other accounts.

Overflow of `i64` is out of scope and need not be handled.

# Instructions

In this exercise you will model a binary tree of integers and answer a few questions about it.

A tree is described by a *level-order* list: a slice of `Option<i32>`. Index 0 is the root. For the node at index `i`, its left child sits at index `2 * i + 1` and its right child at index `2 * i + 2`.

- An empty slice, or a slice whose first element is `None`, describes the empty tree.
- An index past the end of the slice describes a missing child.
- A `None` at index `i` means "no node here"; any values stored at that node's would-be child positions are ignored.

Implement the following methods on `BinaryTree`:

- `from_level_order(values: &[Option<i32>]) -> Self` builds the tree.
- `is_empty(&self) -> bool`
- `len(&self) -> usize` counts the nodes in the tree.
- `height(&self) -> usize` is the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. The empty tree has height 0 and a single node has height 1.
- `leaves(&self) -> usize` counts nodes with no children. A single-node tree has one leaf.
- `in_order(&self) -> Vec<i32>` lists the values using an in-order traversal (left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree).
- `contains(&self, target: i32) -> bool` reports whether any node holds `target`.

Values are not sorted and may repeat; `contains` must search the whole tree.

Example: `[Some(2), Some(1), Some(3)]` is a root 2 with children 1 and 3, so `in_order` gives `[1, 2, 3]`, `height` is 2 and `leaves` is 2.

Example: `[Some(2), None, Some(3), Some(4)]` has root 2 with only a right child 3; the `Some(4)` at index 3 is ignored because index 1 is `None`.

# Instructions

Implement a simple tokenizer for a small expression language. The tokenizer is exposed as a function:

`pub fn tokenize(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<Token>, TokenizeError>`

It scans `input` from left to right and returns the list of tokens in order.

## Token types

The `Token` enum has these variants:

- `Number(i64)` — one or more ASCII digits, parsed as a signed 64-bit integer.
- `Ident(String)` — an identifier: starts with an ASCII letter or underscore, followed by zero or more ASCII letters, digits, or underscores.
- `Plus`, `Minus`, `Star`, `Slash` — the operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`.
- `LParen`, `RParen` — `(` and `)`.
- `Comma` — `,`.
- `Assign` — `=`.
- `EqEq`, `BangEq`, `Less`, `LessEq`, `Greater`, `GreaterEq` — the operators `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`.

## Scanning rules

- Whitespace (` `, `\t`, `\n`, `\r`) is skipped.
- Numbers and identifiers are recognised greedily. For example, `12abc` becomes `Number(12)` followed by `Ident("abc")`.
- The two-character operators `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=` are recognised before their single-character counterparts. Thus `<=` is `LessEq`, not `Less` followed by `Assign`.
- A lone `!` is not a valid token and must produce an error.
- Any character that does not start a valid token produces an error.

## Errors

`TokenizeError` has these variants:

- `UnexpectedCharacter(char, usize)` — the character and the byte index where it occurred.
- `InvalidNumber(String, usize)` — the offending digit string and the byte index where the number started. This occurs when a sequence of digits cannot be parsed as an `i64`.

The function returns `Ok(tokens)` for valid input and `Err(error)` for the first problem encountered.

Implement three functions that operate on two-dimensional integer matrices (grids of `i32`).

A matrix is represented as `Vec<Vec<i32>>`. A matrix is **rectangular** when every row has the same length. An empty matrix (no rows) and a matrix whose rows are all empty are both considered rectangular.

Define a public error type:

```rust
pub enum MatrixError {
    NotRectangular,
}
```

## 1. `spiral_order`

```rust
pub fn spiral_order(matrix: &[Vec<i32>]) -> Result<Vec<i32>, MatrixError>
```

Return all elements visited in a clockwise spiral that starts at the top-left cell and moves:

1. right along the top row,
2. down the right column,
3. left along the bottom row,
4. up the left column,

then inward, repeating until every cell has been visited.

Edge cases:

- An empty matrix returns `Ok(vec![])`.
- A matrix where every row is empty returns `Ok(vec![])`.
- A non-rectangular matrix returns `Err(MatrixError::NotRectangular)`.
- Single-row and single-column matrices are valid and must be handled without visiting a cell twice.

## 2. `generate_spiral`

```rust
pub fn generate_spiral(rows: usize, cols: usize) -> Vec<Vec<i32>>
```

Build a `rows` by `cols` matrix filled with the consecutive integers `1..=rows*cols` in clockwise spiral order (the same order `spiral_order` would traverse), starting at the top-left with `1`. Rectangular outputs are allowed.

- If either dimension is `0`, return an empty matrix (`rows` empty rows when `rows == 0`, otherwise `rows` rows that are each empty when `cols == 0`).

## 3. `rotate_clockwise`

```rust
pub fn rotate_clockwise(matrix: &[Vec<i32>]) -> Result<Vec<Vec<i32>>, MatrixError>
```

Return the matrix rotated 90 degrees clockwise, so element at row `r`, column `c` moves to row `c`, column `rows - 1 - r` in the result.

- An empty matrix returns `Ok(vec![])`.
- A non-rectangular matrix returns `Err(MatrixError::NotRectangular)`.

Implement three functions for permutations of a multiset of `u32` values.

A multiset is represented by a slice of values; order in the input is irrelevant. The distinct permutations are ordered lexicographically by comparing their elements from left to right, using ordinary numeric order. Ranks are zero-based.

- `count_distinct_permutations(items)` returns the number of distinct permutations of the multiset. The empty multiset has exactly one permutation: the empty sequence.
- `unrank_permutation(items, rank)` returns `Some(permutation)` for the `rank`-th distinct permutation in lexicographic order, or `None` if `rank` is out of range.
- `rank_permutation(items, permutation)` returns `Some(rank)` if `permutation` is a permutation of `items`, and `None` otherwise. A valid permutation must contain exactly the same values with the same multiplicities as `items`; order matters for the rank.

Duplicates must not produce duplicate permutations. For example, the multiset `[1, 1, 2]` has three distinct permutations in lexicographic order: `[1, 1, 2]`, `[1, 2, 1]`, and `[2, 1, 1]`.

Counts may be large; for exercise inputs they fit in `u128`. Inputs are not assumed to be sorted. Treat the empty slice as valid for all operations. Do not mutate the input slices.

# Instructions

Implement a generic priority queue type named `PriorityQueue<T>`.

A priority queue stores items together with integer priorities. The item with the greatest priority value is considered the highest priority; negative priorities are allowed. Items with equal priorities are served in FIFO order: among items with the same priority, the item pushed earliest is popped first.

Required API:

- `PriorityQueue::new()` creates an empty queue.
- `push(&mut self, item: T, priority: i32)` adds an item with the given priority.
- `pop(&mut self) -> Option<T>` removes and returns the highest-priority item, or `None` if the queue is empty.
- `peek(&self) -> Option<&T>` returns a reference to the highest-priority item without removing it, or `None` if the queue is empty.
- `len(&self) -> usize` returns the number of stored items.
- `is_empty(&self) -> bool` returns whether the queue has no items.
- `clear(&mut self)` removes all items.
- `Default::default()` must produce an empty queue.

The item type must not be required to implement `Ord`; ordering is determined only by the priority and, for ties, insertion order. Pushing a higher-priority item may cause it to be popped before earlier lower-priority items. After clearing, the queue can be reused normally.

Create a generic `RingBuffer<T>` type with these methods:

- `clear()` removes all stored values and leaves the buffer empty.

Reads must return values in insertion order. Indices wrap around at the end of the backing storage. The buffer must work with non-Copy values, and `clear` must drop the values it removes.

# Instructions

Implement a fixed-capacity ring buffer that stores values in first-in, first-out order.

Create a generic type `RingBuffer<T>` with these methods:

- `new(capacity: usize) -> Self` creates an empty buffer that can hold at most `capacity` values. A capacity of zero is allowed.
- `write(&mut self, value: T) -> Result<(), T>` adds `value` to the buffer. If the buffer is full, return `Err(value)` and leave the buffer unchanged. Otherwise return `Ok(())`.
- `read(&mut self) -> Option<T>` removes and returns the oldest value. If the buffer is empty, return `None`.
- `overwrite(&mut self, value: T)` adds `value`. If the buffer is not full, this behaves like a successful `write`. If it is full, the oldest value is discarded, `value` is stored, and the remaining values keep their order.
- `clear(&mut self)` removes all values and leaves the buffer empty.
- `len(&self) -> usize` returns the number of stored values.
- `is_empty(&self) -> bool` returns whether no values are stored.
- `is_full(&self) -> bool` returns whether the buffer has reached its capacity.

Edge cases:

- A buffer with capacity zero is both empty and full.
- On a zero-capacity buffer, `write` returns `Err(value)`, `read` returns `None`, and `overwrite` does nothing.
- After `clear`, the buffer can be reused.
- Values may be of any type; the buffer must not require `Clone` or `Copy`.
- `write` must never evict existing values. Only `overwrite` may discard the oldest value when full.

# Instructions

Implement a small in-memory bank that models accounts as objects managed by a Bank. Use only the standard library.

Account IDs are u32 values. The first successful open_account call returns 1, the next returns 2, and so on. IDs are never reused, even after an account is closed.

Public API:

Bank::new() -> Bank
Bank::open_account(owner: &str, initial_deposit: i64) -> Result<u32, BankError>
Bank::deposit(id: u32, amount: i64) -> Result<i64, BankError>
Bank::withdraw(id: u32, amount: i64) -> Result<i64, BankError>
Bank::transfer(from: u32, to: u32, amount: i64) -> Result<(), BankError>
Bank::balance(id: u32) -> Result<i64, BankError>
Bank::available_balance(id: u32) -> Result<i64, BankError>
Bank::set_overdraft(id: u32, limit: i64) -> Result<(), BankError>
Bank::close_account(id: u32) -> Result<i64, BankError>
Bank::is_closed(id: u32) -> Result<bool, BankError>
Bank::owner(id: u32) -> Result<&str, BankError>
Bank::account_count() -> usize

BankError must have exactly these variants: AccountNotFound, AccountClosed, InvalidAmount, InvalidOwner, InsufficientFunds, SameAccount.

Rules:

- open_account rejects an owner that is empty after trimming whitespace with InvalidOwner. It stores the owner exactly as supplied. A negative initial deposit is InvalidAmount. Owner validation happens before initial-deposit validation. A new account starts open, with the given balance and an overdraft limit of 0.
- deposit and withdraw require amount > 0; otherwise return InvalidAmount before looking up the account. They require an existing open account. deposit returns the new balance. withdraw permits the balance to go as low as the negative of the overdraft limit; returns the new balance, or InsufficientFunds if that limit would be exceeded.
- available_balance for an open account is balance plus overdraft limit. For a closed account it is 0.
- set_overdraft requires limit >= 0 and an existing open account. It changes only the limit, not the balance. The limit check happens before account lookup.
- transfer checks in this order: amount > 0; from and to are different; from exists and is open; to exists and is open; the source has enough available balance. On any error no balance changes. Same account is SameAccount. Missing accounts are AccountNotFound. Closed accounts are AccountClosed. Too little available balance is InsufficientFunds. On success it moves the amount and returns Ok.
- close_account requires an existing open account. It returns that account's current balance, which may be negative, then sets the balance and overdraft limit to 0 and marks the account closed. Closing an already closed account returns AccountClosed.
- Closed accounts reject deposit, withdraw, set_overdraft, close_account, and use as either side of a transfer. Queries balance, available_balance, owner, and is_closed still work. balance is 0 for a closed account.
- Every method that takes an account ID returns AccountNotFound for an unknown ID.
- account_count returns the total number of accounts ever opened, including closed accounts.

Implement a graph data structure using an adjacency map. The graph is undirected and unweighted. Nodes are represented by unsigned 32-bit integers.

Your task is to implement the `Graph` struct with the following methods:

- `new()`: Creates an empty graph.
- `add_edge(u, v)`: Adds an undirected edge between nodes `u` and `v`. If either node does not exist, it is added. If the edge already exists, it is not added again. Self-loops (where `u == v`) are ignored.
- `neighbors(node)`: Returns a sorted vector of all nodes adjacent to the given `node`. If the node does not exist in the graph, returns an empty vector.
- `shortest_path(start, end)`: Returns the shortest path from `start` to `end` as a vector of nodes, including both `start` and `end`. If no path exists, or if either node is not in the graph, returns `None`. If `start == end` and the node exists, returns `Some(vec![start])`. The path should be the shortest in terms of number of edges. If multiple shortest paths exist, any one is acceptable.
- `connected_components()`: Returns a vector of connected components. Each component is a sorted vector of its nodes. The outer vector is sorted by the first node of each component. For an empty graph, returns an empty vector.

Edge cases:
- Empty graph.
- Adding duplicate edges.
- Self-loops.
- Nodes not present in the graph.

- `enqueue(item)` adds `item` to the back. This is the queue enqueue operation.

- `is_empty()` returns `true` only when there are no stored items.

For example, if items are added with `push` or `enqueue`, then `pop` removes the most recently added remaining item, while `dequeue` removes the oldest remaining item. # Instructions

Implement an undirected graph data structure backed by an adjacency map (a HashMap mapping each node name to the list of its neighbors).

Complete the Graph type in the starter file. It exposes the following methods:

- `Graph::new()` creates an empty graph.
- `add_node(&mut self, node: &str)` adds a node if it is not already present. Adding a node that already exists does nothing.
- `add_edge(&mut self, from: &str, to: &str)` adds an undirected edge between the two names. Both endpoints are created if they are missing. If from equals to, the node is added (if missing) but no edge is recorded. If the edge already exists in either direction it is ignored, so the graph never contains duplicate edges.
- `neighbors(&self, node: &str) -> Vec<String>` returns the neighbors of node sorted alphabetically. Returns an empty vector if node is not in the graph.
- `degree(&self, node: &str) -> Option<usize>` returns Some(n) where n is the number of distinct neighbors, or None if the node is not in the graph. Self-edges are never counted because they are ignored.
- `node_count(&self) -> usize` returns the number of nodes in the graph.
- `has_path(&self, from: &str, to: &str) -> bool` returns whether there is a path from one node to the other. Because the graph is undirected this is symmetric. Returns true when from equals to and that node exists. Returns false when either endpoint is missing.
- `is_connected(&self) -> bool` returns whether every node can reach every other node. For an empty graph and for a graph with exactly one node this is true.

## Examples

After adding the edges "a"-"b" and "b"-"c", neighbors("b") is the sorted list ["a", "c"], has_path("a", "c") is true, and is_connected() is true.

## Edge cases

- Self-edges must be ignored.
- Adding the same edge twice must not create duplicate entries.
- Neighbors must be returned in alphabetical order.
- An isolated node added with add_node makes the graph disconnected.
- Querying a node that is not in the graph must not panic.

Implement a simple tokenizer for a small expression language. Provide:

- `pub fn tokenize(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<Token>, TokenizeError>`
- `pub enum Token` with variants `Identifier(String)`, `Number(i64)`, `StringLiteral(String)`, `Operator(String)`, and `Punctuation(char)`
- `pub enum TokenizeError` with variants `UnexpectedCharacter(char)`, `UnterminatedString`, `InvalidEscape(char)`, and `NumberTooLarge`

`Token` and `TokenizeError` should derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, and `Eq`.

Scan input left to right. Skip any Unicode whitespace between tokens. Whitespace inside a string literal is part of the string. Return tokens in source order.

Rules:

- Identifier: starts with an ASCII letter or `_`, and continues with ASCII alphanumeric characters or `_`. There is no keyword special-casing.
- Number: one or more ASCII digits, parsed as `i64`. Leading zeros are allowed but not preserved. If the digits do not fit in `i64`, return `NumberTooLarge`. A leading minus is not part of the number; `-12` becomes operator `-` followed by number `12`.
- String literal: begins with `"`. It ends at the next unescaped `"`. Escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, and `\r` are decoded. Any other escaped character returns `InvalidEscape(c)`. Reaching the end of input before the closing quote returns `UnterminatedString`. Raw newlines are allowed inside strings; any character other than `"` and `\` is included literally.
- Operator: one of `+ - * / % = < > ! & |`. The two-character operators `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, and `||` are recognized when both characters are adjacent. Otherwise each operator character becomes its own `Operator` token containing that character as a `String`.
- Punctuation: one of `( ) [ ] { } , ; : .` as `Punctuation(char)`.
- Any other character returns `UnexpectedCharacter(c)`.

For example, `foo(42)` produces `Identifier("foo")`, `Punctuation('(')`, `Number(42)`, `Punctuation(')')`. Empty or whitespace-only input returns `Ok(vec![])`.

Given a four-digit number, sort its digits in descending order to form one number and in ascending order to form another, then subtract the smaller from the larger. - `8730 - 0378 = 8352`
- `8532 - 2358 = 6174`

Behaviour and edge cases:

- Return `Some(0)` if `n` is already `6174`.

- Return `None` if the digits of `n` are all identical, because the routine then reaches `0` and stays there forever. This includes `0` and repdigits such as `1111` or `9999`.

# Instructions

Write a tokenizer that turns a source string into a list of tokens, or reports the first lexical error it finds.

## Required API

Define these public items exactly. The tests refer to them by name.

- `pub fn tokenize(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<Token>, TokenizerError>`

- `pub enum Token` with the variants `Identifier(String)`, `Number(String)`, `Str(String)`, `Op(Op)`, `Punct(Punct)`

- `pub enum Op` with the variants `Plus`, `Minus`, `Star`, `Slash`, `Assign`, `Eq`, `Ne`, `Not`, `Lt`, `Le`, `Gt`, `Ge`

- `pub enum Punct` with the variants `LParen`, `RParen`, `LBrace`, `RBrace`, `Comma`, `Semicolon`

- `pub enum TokenizerError` with the variants `UnexpectedCharacter { ch: char, pos: usize }`, `UnterminatedString { pos: usize }`, `UnterminatedComment { pos: usize }`, and `InvalidEscape { ch: char, pos: usize }`

All of these must derive `Debug`, `Clone`, and `PartialEq` so they can be compared with `==`.

## Positions

Every `pos` field is a zero-based index counted in Unicode scalar values (chars), not bytes, measured from the start of the input.

## Scanning rules

Skip whitespace: space, tab, carriage return, and newline produce no tokens.

Line comments: two consecutive slashes `//` start a comment that lasts until the next newline or the end of input. It produces no tokens. A slash that is not followed by another slash or by an asterisk is the `Slash` operator.

Block comments: a slash followed by an asterisk `/*` starts a comment that ends at the next `*/`. Block comments do not nest; the first `*/` closes it, and the closing pair is consumed. If the input ends before a closing `*/` is found, return `UnterminatedComment` with `pos` set to the index of the opening slash.

Identifiers: an identifier begins with an ASCII letter `a-z` or `A-Z` or an underscore, and continues with ASCII letters, ASCII digits, or underscores. Non-ASCII letters are not identifiers and produce an error.

Numbers: one or more ASCII digits, optionally followed by a single dot and one or more ASCII digits. A dot only belongs to a number when it is immediately followed by a digit, so `1.` yields `Number("1")` and then an `UnexpectedCharacter` error at the dot, and `.5` is an `UnexpectedCharacter` error at the dot. The token stores the text exactly as written, including the dot, for example `"3.14"` or `"007"`. No signs, exponents, or separators are recognized.

String literals: a double quote begins a string that ends at the next unescaped double quote. The token stores the decoded contents without the surrounding quotes. A backslash introduces exactly one of these escapes: `\n` newline, `\t` tab, `\r` carriage return, `\\` backslash, `\"` double quote. Any other character after a backslash is `InvalidEscape`, where `ch` is that character and `pos` is the index of the backslash. A raw newline inside a string is allowed and becomes part of the value. If the input ends before the closing quote (including when a backslash is the last character), return `UnterminatedString` with `pos` set to the index of the opening quote.

Operators, matched longest first: `+` Plus, `-` Minus, `*` Star, `/` Slash, `=` Assign but `==` Eq, `!` Not but `!=` Ne, `<` Lt but `<=` Le, `>` Gt but `>=` Ge.

# Instructions

Implement a fixed-capacity ring buffer, also called a circular buffer, that stores values in first-in, first-out order.

Create a generic type `RingBuffer<T>` in this file. A buffer is created with `RingBuffer::new(capacity)`. The capacity must be at least 1; `new(0)` must panic. The buffer must work for any `T`, including non-`Copy` types such as `String`.

The buffer exposes these methods:

- `capacity(&self) -> usize` returns the maximum number of stored items.
- `len(&self) -> usize` returns the current number of stored items.
- `is_empty(&self) -> bool` is true when no items are stored.
- `is_full(&self) -> bool` is true when `len() == capacity()`.
- `write(&mut self, item: T) -> Result<(), T>` appends an item to the newest end. If there is room it stores the item and returns `Ok(())`. If the buffer is full it stores nothing and returns `Err(item)` with the original item.
- `overwrite(&mut self, item: T) -> Option<T>` appends when there is room and returns `None`. When full, it replaces the oldest item with the new item, returns the replaced oldest item as `Some(old)`, and makes the new item the newest item.
- `read(&mut self) -> Option<T>` removes and returns the oldest item, or `None` if the buffer is empty.
- `peek(&self) -> Option<&T>` returns a reference to the oldest item without removing it, or `None` if the buffer is empty.
- `clear(&mut self)` removes all items, leaving an empty buffer with the same capacity.
- `iter(&self) -> Iter<'_, T>` returns an iterator over references to the stored items, from oldest to newest. The iterator must implement `Iterator` and `ExactSizeIterator`; its length must equal the buffer length.

After a read, the next-oldest item becomes the oldest. Writes and overwrites must continue to preserve FIFO order as the internal storage wraps around. For example, in a capacity-3 buffer holding 1, 2, 3, a read removes 1; writing 4 then gives 2, 3, 4. Overwriting 5 into a full 2, 3, 4 buffer returns `Some(2)` and leaves 3, 4, 5.

Implement Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe.

The board is nine 3x3 microboards arranged as a 3x3 macroboard. Microboard and cell indices are 0 through 8 in row-major order. Players alternate placing X and O, with X moving first. A move is a pair (board, cell).

The first move may be in any microboard. After a move, the next player must play in the microboard whose index equals the cell index just played, unless that microboard is already won or full. In that case the next player may choose any playable microboard.

A microboard is won by three matching marks in a row, column, or diagonal. It is closed when it is won or full. A closed microboard cannot receive more moves. A full microboard with no winner is a draw and is closed.

The game is won when a player wins three microboards in a row, column, or diagonal in the macroboard. If there is no macroboard winner and every microboard is closed, the game is a draw. Play must stop as soon as the game is won or drawn.

Provide these public items:

- Player: X or O. It has other() for the opposite player and symbol() returning 'X' or 'O'.
- Cell: Empty, X, or O.
- Status: InProgress, Won(Player), or Draw.
- UltimateTicTacToe with new().

UltimateTicTacToe methods:

- next_player() returns the player who must move next.
- active_board() returns Some(index) when the next move is forced to that microboard, and None when the next player may choose any playable microboard. It returns None after the game is over.
- get(board, cell) returns Some(Cell) for in-range indices and None otherwise.
- legal_moves() returns all legal moves as (board, cell) pairs, sorted by board and then cell. It returns an empty vector after the game is over.
- play(board, cell) validates and makes a move. It returns Err for out-of-range indices, a finished game, ignoring the forced microboard, a closed microboard, or an occupied cell. On success it places the current player's mark, updates the forced microboard from the played cell index, switching to no forced microboard if that microboard is closed, and switches players.
- status() returns the current Status.

new() creates an empty game with X to move and no forced microboard. A move that wins a microboard or fills it closes it. A move that wins the macroboard or makes a draw ends the game. Any invalid move must not change the game. The exact error text is not specified.
